cards.title: Can membership queries always be removed from agnostic testable learning?
cards.formal: For every represented Boolean concept-class family C_n on finite encoded domains X_n and every target distribution family consisting of one specified distribution D_n on each X_n, does agnostic testable learnability with membership queries imply agnostic testable learnability using only independent labeled examples, with polynomial overhead in running time? Both learners must retain the same target distributions, proper-hypothesis convention and additive excess-error guarantee.
cards.why: Would determine whether chosen-label access can substantially accelerate learning when distributional assumptions must also be checked. It isolates the computational cost of reliable rejection from the cost of prediction itself.

references.title: Limitations of Membership Queries in Testable Learning

cards.definitions: A concept class C_n is a nonempty set of functions X_n→{0,1}, with a fixed common input and hypothesis representation in both models. Data consist of independent examples (x,f*(x)), where x follows an unknown distribution P on X_n and f*:X_n→{0,1} is an arbitrary fixed labeling function, not necessarily in C_n. A membership query chooses any x∈X_n and receives f*(x); repeated queries have the same label. For h∈C_n, define err_P(h)=Pr_{x∼P}[h(x)≠f*(x)] and opt=inf_{g∈C_n}err_P(g). Given accuracy ε and failure probability δ, a testable learner returns h∈C_n or the rejection symbol ⊥. Soundness holds for every P and f*: Pr[h≠⊥ and err_P(h)>opt+ε]≤δ. Completeness holds whenever P=D_n: Pr[h=⊥]≤δ. Probabilities are over samples and the learner’s randomness. This explicitly uses the usual joint bad-output event for the source’s informal “if it outputs” guarantee, not conditioning on a potentially extremely rare acceptance event. The sample-only learner has no membership oracle and satisfies the same two guarantees. Running time includes sample/query processing and writing the hypothesis; encodings and any given target-distribution description are unchanged. Polynomial overhead is understood in the standard parameterized sense, accounting for input size, 1/ε and log(1/δ) as well as the query learner’s time. The agnostic coefficient on opt is exactly one; an unspecified constant multiple is the different semi-agnostic model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication by constructing sample-only testable learners with polynomially related resource bounds and the same agnostic guarantee, or exhibit a class/distribution family with a superpolynomial separation between the two testable-learning access models. Reducing query-based testable learning merely to ordinary sample-based agnostic learning is insufficient, because ordinary learning lacks soundness outside the target distribution.

context_blocks.title: The learner may refuse an unsupported prediction
context_blocks.text: A distribution-specific learner is accurate only under its assumed data distribution. A testable learner may reject, but a returned predictor must have near-optimal error even when that assumption fails. On the intended distribution, it must usually return a predictor.

context_blocks.title: Chosen queries can probe rare inputs
context_blocks.text: If the data distribution rarely samples a certain input, ordinary examples may never reveal its label. Membership queries allow the learner to inspect it directly. The conjecture asks whether this extra access can still give more than a polynomial speedup once the testability requirements are imposed.

context_blocks.title: Agnostic does not mean the labels change on repeated queries
context_blocks.text: The unknown labeling function may disagree with every concept in the class. The benchmark therefore allows its unavoidable error opt. In the paper’s membership-query model, however, a fixed input has a fixed label; this differs from independently resampling noisy labels on every oracle call.

context_blocks.title: The known reduction stops at ordinary learning
context_blocks.text: The paper gives a reduction through refutation leading to ordinary sample-based agnostic learning, under the quantitative hypotheses stated in its theorem. That conclusion does not supply the missing tester. Conjecture 6 asks for the stronger sample-only testable learner.

context_blocks.title: Testing can itself dominate the cost
context_blocks.text: The source uses monotone Boolean functions under the uniform distribution to illustrate the gap: sample-based testable learning needs exponentially many samples, while ordinary agnostic learning and refutation have subexponential bounds. Thus an ordinary-learning simulation does not settle the conjecture.

cards.title: Cloning random-circuit states without first learning their circuits
cards.formal: Can one exploit the structure of random quantum-circuit output states to clone them more effectively than known learning-based algorithms, even with subexponential running time and only polynomially many input copies? The source’s algorithm question is parameterized by the circuit ensemble and the desired fidelity and success probability; it does not select a single complete benchmark.
cards.why: Would clarify whether producing additional quantum samples is computationally easier than identifying their preparation circuit. That distinction affects cryptographic assumptions based on the difficulty of learning or cloning efficiently preparable states.
cards.status_note: Source model and algorithm question, universal-cloning theorem statement and later ensemble-cloning result checked through 11 September 2026. No matching resolution was located. The source’s open-ended algorithm comparison still needs a fixed quantitative benchmark.

sentences: An unknown random circuit prepares a quantum state, and the algorithm receives only polynomially many copies of that state.
The task is to output one more copy while keeping the whole joint output close to the desired tensor product.
Universal cloning has global fidelity (k+1)/(2ⁿ+k), which is exponentially small for polynomially many input copies.
The source asks whether circuit structure permits better direct cloning, even in subexponential time.
A concrete circuit ensemble, fidelity and success target, and comparison with learning-based algorithms still need to be specified.

cards.definitions: A sampled n-qubit circuit C prepares the pure state |C⟩=C|0ⁿ⟩. A cloning algorithm receives k copies |C⟩^{⊗k}, with k polynomial in n, and outputs (k+1) registers of n qubits. It receives neither C’s classical description nor a preparation oracle. For output density operator ρ, global squared fidelity with the desired copies is F_C(ρ)=⟨C|^{⊗(k+1)}ρ|C⟩^{⊗(k+1)}. This checks the entire joint output, not each register separately. A high-probability formulation also specifies the distribution of output branches and functions ε(n),δ(n): the source’s No-Cloning assumption says that for every polynomial-time quantum algorithm and polynomial k, the probability of a branch with fidelity at least ε is at most δ for all sufficiently large n. Its probability includes the random circuit and the algorithm’s output randomness. This tail guarantee differs from specifying only expected fidelity. Subexponential time means 2^{o(n)} relative to the number of qubits. The paper offers depth (log n)² one-dimensional brickwork circuits as a motivating ensemble, rather than fixing that as the only allowed family in the selected algorithm question. “Random circuit” must ultimately include a gate-sampling and precision convention.
cards.answer_criterion: First fix the ensemble, copy budget, running time, fidelity statistic and success threshold. Then give and analyze an algorithm meeting that guarantee, or prove an appropriately scoped lower bound. Any claimed improvement over learning-based cloning must have a quantitative comparison; merely omitting a classical circuit description from the output is not such a comparison.

context_blocks.title: The output is one joint approximation
context_blocks.text: For one qubit, a pair of correlated registers can have plausible individual marginals without being two copies of the desired pure state. The global-fidelity criterion checks the entire tensor-product target, including the retained input copies.

context_blocks.title: The universal benchmark is exponentially small
context_blocks.text: Werner’s theorem gives exact optimal worst-case k→k+1 global fidelity (k+1)/(2ⁿ+k) for arbitrary n-qubit pure states. For polynomial k this is exponentially small. The ITCS display simplifies a ratio of binomial coefficients to a denominator 2ⁿ; the exact denominator is 2ⁿ+k. The asymptotic conclusion is unchanged.

context_blocks.title: Efficient preparation is extra structure
context_blocks.text: A state drawn from a chosen low-depth circuit ensemble occupies a restricted part of the full pure-state space. Universal no-cloning optimality alone does not rule out better performance on that ensemble. The question concerns what can be extracted from copies when the preparation circuit is unknown.

context_blocks.title: Learning and cloning have different required outputs
context_blocks.text: A learner must produce a classical description that prepares a good approximation. A cloner needs only the extra quantum output. This leaves room for a computational separation, but the phrase “without learning first” needs a measurable performance target before it defines a theorem.

context_blocks.title: A later ensemble theorem uses a different input and target
context_blocks.text: The June 2026 ensemble-cloning paper studies copies of a purification and matching copies of states obtained by a random projection of part of it. That result does not establish a lower bound for the full-state random-circuit cloning task posed here.

cards.title: Efficient Reed–Solomon list decoding beyond the Johnson radius
cards.formal: Can some asymptotic family of Reed–Solomon codes be list decoded in polynomial time against fully adversarial errors beyond the Johnson radius n−√(nk), where n is block length and k is message dimension? The selected passage leaves the family’s parameter regime and required improvement unspecified; those choices must be fixed before this becomes one nontrivial asymptotic algorithmic claim.
cards.why: Targets the gap between the information-theoretic potential of Reed–Solomon codes and algorithms that recover all nearby messages under arbitrary corruption. The family and radius regime determine whether a claimed improvement is a substantial decoding advance.
cards.status_note: Primary passage, latest arXiv version record and subsequent searches checked through 11 September 2026. The source still identifies the general algorithmic gap, but does not fix one asymptotic benchmark. No matching general resolution was located.

importance.reason: An important algorithmic gap for algebraic error-correcting codes. Existing numerical score retained.

sentences: Reed–Solomon codes encode a polynomial by its values at distinct field points.
The source asks for efficient list decoding under fully adversarial errors beyond n−√(nk) errors.
A small possible list does not by itself give an algorithm for finding it.
The paper’s semi-adversarial results rely on randomness in part of the corruption and do not supply the desired worst-case guarantee.
The asymptotic family, rate and size of the radius improvement still need to be fixed to exclude trivial small-message families.

cards.definitions: For a prime power q, distinct evaluation points a₁,…,a_n∈𝔽_q and 1≤k≤n≤q, RS_q(a₁,…,a_n;k) consists of (f(a₁),…,f(a_n)) for all f∈𝔽_q[x] with degree less than k. Its rate is R=k/n, its message is the k coefficients of f, and symbols are field elements. Hamming distance d_H counts coordinates with unequal symbols. A list decoder at integer radius t must, for every received word y∈𝔽_q^n, output all degree-<k polynomials f with d_H((f(aᵢ))ᵢ,y)≤t. It may remove extraneous candidates by checking this inequality. Fully adversarial means there is no random-error or typical-received-word promise. The source writes the Johnson threshold as n−√(nk), equivalently relative radius 1−√R, with integer rounding needed for an exact radius. List decodability only bounds how many candidates exist; efficient list decoding also finds them, and writing the list counts toward time. A bit-complexity claim must account for n, k, log q, field representation and evaluation points, rather than treating a field of arbitrarily large description as free. A subclass here is a selected family of RS codes; the ordinary RS definition itself is not replaced by a folded-symbol or different-distance metric.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a nontrivial growing family and all rate, alphabet, radius and success parameters, then construct a decoder which returns the full list within the claimed polynomial cost for every received word. Alternatively, formulate and prove an impossibility covering all families allowed by that specification. Combinatorial existence of small lists or decoding only random/semi-adversarial errors does not meet the algorithmic target.

context_blocks.title: Why more errors require a list
context_blocks.text: Several messages can be close to the same corrupted word. Returning every nearby message avoids insisting on a unique answer when uniqueness is information-theoretically impossible. The decoder must find the complete nearby list, not only one plausible candidate.

context_blocks.title: The missing bound is now explicit
context_blocks.text: At rate R=1/4, the source’s Johnson threshold is an error fraction of 1/2. Beating it means handling received words with more than half the symbols corrupted while still returning all nearby codewords efficiently. This numerical example explains the threshold; it does not select R=1/4 as the only allowed rate.

context_blocks.title: A small list is different from a fast decoder
context_blocks.text: The source reviews RS families whose combinatorial list-decoding radius exceeds Johnson and can approach capacity. These results show that few answers may exist. They do not by themselves give a polynomial-time way to locate those answers.

context_blocks.title: Semi-adversarial algorithms answer a different guarantee
context_blocks.text: The paper allows some errors to be adversarial and others to have random replacement values. Its interleaved-code result addresses that mixed model. It does not establish the missing full-list guarantee for every adversarial received word.

context_blocks.title: Why the asymptotic regime must be fixed
context_blocks.text: For fixed k and q polynomial in n, there are only q^k message polynomials, so exhaustively listing them is already polynomial time. An unrestricted phrase such as “some subclass” would admit such easy regimes. A useful statement must specify what rate and improvement should persist as n grows.

notes: Recovered the source model and recorded the remaining specification choices.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The source asks for an algorithm for some subclass beyond the Johnson bound, without selecting an asymptotic rate regime, a nonvanishing versus smaller improvement in radius, permitted field-size growth, deterministic versus randomized guarantee, or how the subclass is presented/constructed. These affect whether the task is a substantive asymptotic advance: constant-dimension RS families already have polynomially many messages over polynomial-size fields. Fixing a constant positive rate and a constant radius improvement would be one stronger benchmark, but is not silently substituted for the source’s broader question.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance.
